docs.title: Overwatch
docs.text:
Overwatch assesses software requirements for correctness.

Point it at a directory of requirements and it returns a verdict on whether each one conforms to EARS — the Easy Approach to Requirements Syntax — along with the matched pattern and a short rationale.

Under the hood, the owatch CLI sends the requirement to the Overwatch REST API, which asks a foundation model (via Amazon Bedrock, in-region in eu-west-2) to judge it against the five EARS patterns.

docs.title: Verdicts
docs.text: Verdict Meaning Compliant The requirement matches one of the five EARS patterns; matched_pattern names which. Non-Compliant It is a requirement, but fits no EARS pattern. Indeterminate It cannot be judged as a requirement at all — empty, a question, a fragment.

docs.title: The five EARS patterns
docs.text: Pattern Shape Ubiquitous The <system> shall <response>. Event-driven When <trigger>, the <system> shall <response>. State-driven While <state>, the <system> shall <response>. Unwanted behaviour If <condition>, then the <system> shall <response>. Optional feature Where <feature>, the <system> shall <response>.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Installation — get the owatch binary.
  • Getting started — configuration and a first assessment.
  • CLI reference — every command and flag, generated from the CLI itself.

Project status

Overwatch is in early development. Access currently requires credentials provisioned by the operator of an Overwatch deployment — see Getting started.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Overwatch can only be used by requesting an account from support.owatch@proton.me.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
A released owatch binary needs no configuration: the API URL, Cognito client ID, and AWS region of the Overwatch deployment are embedded at build time.

owatch login

You'll be prompted for your username and password (and, on first login, for a new password). On success the CLI stores a refresh token in a credentials file — ~/.config/owatch/credentials.json on Linux, ~/Library/Application Support/owatch/credentials.json on macOS, %AppData%\owatch\credentials.json on Windows — and prints its path. The token lasts 30 days; when it expires, run owatch login again.

Environment variables override the embedded values and the stored token — useful for CI or for pointing at a different deployment:

Variable What it overrides OWATCH_API_URL Base URL of the Overwatch REST API. COGNITO_CLIENT_ID Client ID of the deployment's Cognito user pool app client. AWS_REGION Region the Cognito pool lives in (e.g. eu-west-2). OWATCH_REFRESH_TOKEN The refresh token stored by owatch login.

docs.title: The requirements directory
docs.text:
Requirements live in YAML files: a list of entries, each with a free-form id, the requirement text, and an optional list of tags.

- id: REQ_001
  requirement: When a user submits a requirement, the Overwatch REST API shall return an assessment.
  tags: [api, assess]
- id: REQ_002
  requirement: The system should probably be fast.

IDs must be non-empty and contain only letters, digits, _ or -, so they stay unambiguous in YAML, logs, and error messages.

Those files live together in a directory, which is the unit Overwatch reads. Every .yaml and .yml file directly inside it is read, and anything else is ignored:

requirements/
  requirements.yaml   read
  releases.yaml       read
  legacy.yml          read
  notes.md            ignored
  archive/            ignored

How you split your requirements across those files is entirely your choice. A single file works, and so does one per feature. Overwatch reads nothing into the file names, so splitting or merging files never changes what a requirement means. Use tags to say what a requirement is about.

Requirements are read in ascending file-name order, and in their own order within each file. That is the order assessment results come back in.

Each requirement id must be unique within the directory, whichever file holds it, because the id is how you name a single requirement. A sub-directory is a separate scope with its own ids and tags, and is never read as part of its parent.

docs.title: Tags
docs.text:
Tags say which feature, service or component a requirement is about. They are how you ask which requirements relate to a given part of your system, and a requirement may carry as many as it needs — the one above is about both the API and the assess feature.

Tags are yours to choose. Overwatch defines no vocabulary and reads nothing into your file names, because only you know how your system divides up. The only rules are that a tag is not empty and contains no whitespace, so it stays a single token everywhere it is handled.

Tags are also matched exactly, so api and API are two different tags. Keeping the spelling consistent is what keeps a query over them complete.

Tags are optional. A requirement without them is as valid as it ever was, and nothing about the assessment changes: the verdict depends on the requirement text alone.

docs.title: Checking your requirements
docs.text:
owatch validate checks a requirements directory without calling the API, so it costs nothing to run:

owatch validate ./requirements

It reports every problem it finds, with the file, line and column each was found at:

╷
│ Error: Requirement id is used more than once (duplicate-id)
│
│   on core.yaml line 1, column 7:
│    1: - id: REQ_001
│
│ The id "REQ_001" is already used by the requirement at api.yaml line 1.
│ An id must name exactly one requirement within a directory.
╵
1 error and 0 warnings.

Add --output-file to write the same findings as YAML for a CI job to archive or parse. See Validation rules for what is checked and what each rule name means.

owatch assess runs these checks first and refuses to request anything if they fail, so a mistake in a requirements file never costs an API call to discover.

docs.title: Assessing a requirement
docs.text:
Pass the requirements directory to assess everything in it:

owatch assess ./requirements

Or name a single requirement with -r. The id is looked up across the whole directory, so you do not have to know which file holds it:

owatch assess -r REQ_001 ./requirements

On success the CLI prints the name of a time-stamped assessment file it has written to the current directory:

assessment_20260826_155425_767111.yaml

which contains the result:

- id: REQ_001
  ears_assessment: Compliant
  matched_pattern: Event-driven
  rationale: The requirement follows the When <trigger>, the <system> shall <response> shape.
  tags: [api, assess]

Any tags the requirement carries are copied onto its result, so an assessment file can be filtered by tag on its own. A requirement with no tags produces a result with no tags key.

See Home for what the verdicts and patterns mean, and the CLI reference for every command and flag.

docs.title: When it fails
docs.text:
• OWATCH_API_URL is not set and this build has no embedded default (or any of the other two) — you're running a locally built binary; see the note in Configuration.
  • unknown command "./requirements" — the assess subcommand was omitted: it's owatch assess -r ... <dir>, not owatch -r ....
  • ... is a file: a requirements directory is required — you passed a requirements file. Pass the directory holding it instead.
  • ... holds no requirements files (.yaml or .yml) — the directory exists but nothing in it has a YAML extension. Check you named the directory holding your requirements, not its parent.
  • A block of diagnostics followed by no assessments requested — the requirements directory failed validation, so nothing was sent. Each diagnostic names the rule that raised it; see Validation rules.
  • not logged in or refresh token rejected (expired or revoked) — run owatch login.
  • A 500 from the API — the failure is server-side (the model call itself, or its configuration); nothing the CLI flags can fix. Report it to your operator.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Overwatch ships as a single static binary. The installer detects your platform, verifies the download against the published checksums, and puts owatch on your PATH. No sudo, no admin rights.

docs.title: macOS and Linux
docs.text: curl -fsSL https://github.com/the-common-developers/owatch-releases/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
irm https://github.com/the-common-developers/owatch-releases/releases/latest/download/install.ps1 | iex

Open a new terminal and check it worked:

owatch --version

Then authenticate with the credentials your operator provided:

owatch login

See Getting started for what happens next.

docs.title: What the installer does
docs.text:
1. Detects your OS and CPU architecture (linux_amd64, linux_arm64, darwin_amd64, darwin_arm64, windows_amd64). Windows on ARM gets the amd64 build, which runs under emulation.
  2. Resolves the latest release from owatch-releases.
  3. Downloads the archive and verifies its SHA-256 against checksums.txt. If the digest does not match, or no digest is published for that archive, the installer stops and installs nothing.
  4. Installs to ~/.local/bin (macOS/Linux) or %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\owatch (Windows).
  5. Adds that directory to your PATH if it is not there already.

Re-running the installer upgrades an existing install in place.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Pipe arguments through to the script after -s --:

url=https://github.com/the-common-developers/owatch-releases/releases/latest/download/install.sh

# Install a specific version
curl -fsSL "$url" | sh -s -- --version 0.1.3

# Install somewhere else
curl -fsSL "$url" | sh -s -- --dir /usr/local/bin

# Leave your shell profile alone
curl -fsSL "$url" | sh -s -- --no-modify-path

The same options are available as environment variables, which is usually easier in CI:

Variable Purpose Default OWATCH_VERSION Version to install latest release OWATCH_INSTALL_DIR Install directory ~/.local/bin OWATCH_NO_MODIFY_PATH Set to 1 to skip the PATH update unset OWATCH_BASE_URL Alternative download base URL (internal mirrors) GitHub releases

On Windows, download the script and pass the matching parameters:

$url = 'https://github.com/the-common-developers/owatch-releases/releases/latest/download/install.ps1'
& ([scriptblock]::Create((irm $url))) -Version 0.1.3

Installing into a directory you do not own

The installer never escalates on your behalf. To install somewhere like /usr/local/bin, run the whole script with the permissions it needs: curl -fsSL "$url" | sudo sh -s -- --dir /usr/local/bin.

docs.title: Installing in CI
docs.text:
Pin the version so builds are reproducible, and skip the profile edit:

- name: Install owatch
  run: |
    curl -fsSL https://github.com/the-common-developers/owatch-releases/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
    echo "$HOME/.local/bin" >> "$GITHUB_PATH"
  env:
    OWATCH_VERSION: 0.1.4
    OWATCH_NO_MODIFY_PATH: 1

docs.title: Reviewing the installer first
docs.text:
Piping a script into a shell means trusting the source. The installer verifies what it downloads, but nothing verifies the installer itself — so if you would rather read it before running it:

curl -fsSL https://github.com/the-common-developers/owatch-releases/releases/latest/download/install.sh -o install.sh
less install.sh
sh install.sh

On Windows:

irm https://github.com/the-common-developers/owatch-releases/releases/latest/download/install.ps1 -OutFile install.ps1
notepad install.ps1
./install.ps1

Each release publishes the exact installer that shipped with it, so the copy you review is the copy you run.

docs.title: Uninstalling
docs.text:
The uninstaller removes the binary and the PATH entry the installer added:

curl -fsSL https://github.com/the-common-developers/owatch-releases/releases/latest/download/uninstall.sh | sh

irm https://github.com/the-common-developers/owatch-releases/releases/latest/download/uninstall.ps1 | iex

Your configuration and credentials are left in place, so reinstalling does not mean logging in again. To remove those too:

curl -fsSL https://github.com/the-common-developers/owatch-releases/releases/latest/download/uninstall.sh | sh -s -- --purge

$url = 'https://github.com/the-common-developers/owatch-releases/releases/latest/download/uninstall.ps1'
& ([scriptblock]::Create((irm $url))) -Purge

If you installed somewhere other than the default, tell the uninstaller where: --dir /usr/local/bin (or -InstallDir on Windows).

To do it by hand instead, delete the binary and remove the # Added by the Overwatch CLI installer lines from your shell profile:

rm ~/.local/bin/owatch
rm -rf ~/.config/owatch          # credentials, if you want them gone

Remove-Item "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Programs\owatch" -Recurse
Remove-Item "$env:APPDATA\owatch" -Recurse      # credentials, if you want them gone

docs.title: Manual installation
docs.text:
If you would rather not run a script at all, download the archive directly. Set the version and platform first — platform is one of linux_amd64, linux_arm64, darwin_amd64, darwin_arm64:

VERSION=0.1.4
PLATFORM=darwin_arm64
BASE=https://github.com/the-common-developers/owatch-releases/releases/download/v${VERSION}

curl -LO "${BASE}/owatch_${VERSION}_${PLATFORM}.tar.gz"
curl -LO "${BASE}/checksums.txt"

# Verify (Linux)
sha256sum --check --ignore-missing checksums.txt
# Verify (macOS)
shasum -a 256 --check --ignore-missing checksums.txt

tar -xzf "owatch_${VERSION}_${PLATFORM}.tar.gz"
install -m 755 owatch ~/.local/bin/

On Windows, download owatch_<version>_windows_amd64.zip from the releases page, check its hash against checksums.txt with Get-FileHash, extract owatch.exe, and place it on your PATH.

docs.title: Validation rules
docs.text:
owatch validate checks a requirements directory against the rules below and reports each problem with the file, line and column it was found at. It makes no network calls, so it costs nothing to run as often as you like — and it is the cheapest way to find a problem before owatch assess would bill for one.

$ owatch validate ./requirements
Success! The requirements in ./requirements are valid.

Every rule has a name, which appears in brackets on the diagnostic it raised:

╷
│ Error: Requirement id is used more than once (duplicate-id)
│
│   on core.yaml line 1, column 7:
│    1: - id: REQ_001
│
│ The id "REQ_001" is already used by the requirement at api.yaml line 1.
│ An id must name exactly one requirement within a directory.
╵
1 error and 0 warnings.

owatch assess runs the same rules before it requests anything, so a directory that fails validate will not be assessed.

docs.title: The requirement schema
docs.text:
A requirement holds three fields, and no others:

- id: REQ_001                                    # required
  requirement: The system shall do the thing.    # required
  tags: [cli, assess]                            # optional

An id may hold letters, digits, _ and -. Ids must be unique within a requirements directory, but the same id may be used in a different requirements directory elsewhere.

docs.title: The rules
docs.text:
Rule Severity Raised when invalid-yaml Error A requirements file cannot be parsed as YAML. The other files are still checked. invalid-document Error A requirements file's top-level value is not a list. missing-id Error A requirement has no id, or its id is empty. invalid-id Error An id holds a character other than a letter, a digit, _ or -. duplicate-id Error An id is used by more than one requirement in the directory. Raised against each use after the first. missing-requirement Error A requirement has no requirement text, or its text is empty. invalid-tag Error A tag is empty, or holds whitespace. unknown-field Error A requirement holds a field the schema does not define. no-requirements Error The directory holds requirements files, but none of them holds a requirement.

unknown-field is the rule worth knowing about. A mistyped key is valid YAML and parses without complaint, so without this rule a requirement would quietly lose its tags with nothing to show that it happened:

- id: REQ_001
  requirement: The system shall do the thing.
  tag: cli          # unknown-field: "tag" is ignored, the requirement has no tags

Tags are compared exactly, so API and api are two different tags. That is deliberate: only you know whether your system means them as one.

docs.title: Writing a report file
docs.text:
--output-file writes the diagnostics as YAML, for a CI job to archive or parse. The report is written whether or not anything was found, so a passing run still produces an artefact:

$ owatch validate ./requirements --output-file validation.yaml
validation.yaml

valid: false
error_count: 1
warning_count: 0
diagnostics:
- severity: error
  rule: duplicate-id
  summary: Requirement id is used more than once
  detail: The id "REQ_001" is already used by the requirement at api.yaml line 1.
  range:
    filename: core.yaml
    start:
      line: 1
      column: 7
    end:
      line: 1
      column: 14

The diagnostics go to standard error and the report path to standard output, so the path can be piped somewhere without the diagnostics arriving with it.

docs.title: Exit status
docs.text: validate exits non-zero if any rule raised an error, and zero otherwise. Warnings do not fail a run. No rule raises a warning today; the severity exists because it is a property of a diagnostic rather than of the command, so the report format will not change when the first advisory rule is added.

docs.title: owatch validate
docs.text: Check the requirements in a requirements directory.

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Check every requirement in a requirements directory against the requirement schema and the validation rules, reporting each problem with the file, line and column it was found at.

validate makes no network calls and costs nothing to run, so it is the cheapest way to find a problem before assess would bill for one.

owatch validate <requirements-dir> [flags]

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
-h, --help                 help for validate
  -o, --output-file string   file the YAML validation report is written to (default: no report is written)
